title: Payoff minus premium
objectives: Draw a profit diagram and find the break-even price.

screens.prose: Options are not free. You paid £3.00 today for a call struck at £100.00. At expiry the share is at £110.00, and the diagram shows what the call pays.
screens.question: Counting what you paid, how much did you make?

hints.text: What came in at expiry, and what went out today?
The call pays £10.00 at £110.00.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take what you paid from what the call paid you.

byKey.payoff: That is the payoff. You also paid £3.00 for the call, so take it off.
byKey.added: You added the £3.00. It was money you paid, so it comes off.

explain.text: The call pays $\max(110 - 100, 0) = 10$, and it cost 3. So you made $10 - 3 = 7$. Switching the diagram to profit lowers every point by the 3 you paid.

screens.prose: Now the diagram shows **profit**: what the call pays less what it cost. Move the slider to change the price paid for the call.
screens.question: What does a higher price paid do to the profit line?

options.text: It moves the whole line down by the same amount
It makes the rising part less steep
options.why: You expected the cost to grow with the share price. The price is paid once, so the slope above the strike stays 1.

options.text: It lowers only the rising part, right of the strike
options.why: You moved only the sloped part. The price is paid whatever happens, so the flat part drops too.

options.text: It moves the kink to the right
options.why: The kink stays at the strike, £100.00. What moves right is the point where the line crosses zero.

feedback.correct: Every point drops by the price paid.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move the slider from 0 to 8 and watch the flat part.

explain.text: The price is paid up front, whatever the share does. So every point of the line drops by it, flat part and rising part alike. The crossing with zero slides right as the price rises.

screens.prose: The price of an option is its **premium**, written $c$ for a call. Your **profit** is payoff minus premium. The price at expiry where profit is exactly zero is the **break-even**. The call is struck at £100.00 with $c = \text{£}3.00$.
screens.question: Slide the price at expiry to the break-even.

hints.text: Read the profit in the label as you slide.
Profit is zero where the bold line crosses the axis.
The payoff has to repay the £3.00: $S_T - 100 = 3$, so $S_T = 103$.

feedback.correct: At £103.00 the call pays £3.00, exactly what it cost.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide until the label reads a profit of 0.

byKey.strike: At the strike the call pays 0, and you are still £3.00 down.
byKey.minus: You took the premium off the strike. A call pays for rises, so the share must end £3.00 above it.

explain.text: At £103.00 the call pays $103 - 100 = 3$, which repays the premium. Below it you lose; above it you gain. The hollow marker shows the break-even on the axis.

screens.prose: A call on a pricier share: struck at £250.00, with a premium of £12.50.
screens.question: What is its break-even price at expiry?

hints.text: How far above the strike must the share end to repay the premium?
Each £1.00 above the strike pays £1.00.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The share must end above the strike by the premium.

byKey.strike: At the strike the call pays nothing, and the premium is lost.
byKey.minus: You subtracted the premium. A call recovers its cost only as the share rises.
byKey.premium: That is the premium. The break-even is a share price.

explain.text: Above the strike the payoff grows £1.00 per £1.00, so it reaches the £12.50 premium at $250 + 12.50$. The break-even of a call is $K + c$.

screens.prose: Back to the call struck at £100.00, bought for £3.00. The share could fall a long way before expiry.
screens.question: What is the most you can lose on this call?

options.why: You charged yourself the strike. You pay it only if you choose to exercise, and then you get a share worth more.
You treated the call like a share bought on credit. Below the strike you walk away, so only the premium is gone.
You exercised and paid the premium too. Below the strike you would never exercise.

hints.text: What happens to the call if the share ends far below £100.00?
Read the flat part of the line.
You let the call lapse. The only money gone is the £3.00 paid.

feedback.correct: The flat part sits at −£3.00: the premium is all you can lose.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the profit at a price far below the strike.

explain.text: However low the share ends, the call pays 0 and you lose the premium. So the most a buyer can lose is £3.00. The gain above the strike has no such limit.

screens.prose: A firm grants you a call struck at £100.00 as a bonus, so your premium is £0.00. The profit line is then the payoff line.
screens.question: Where is the break-even of a free call?

options.text: At the strike, £100.00: at or below it you make 0, above it you gain
It has none, since you can never lose
options.why: You looked for a loss. The break-even is where you stop making nothing and start gaining, which is still the strike.
You kept the old premium. With $c = 0$, $K + c = K$.

options.text: At £0.00, where the share is worthless
options.why: At £0.00 the call pays nothing, but so it does everywhere up to £100.00.

hints.text: Use $K + c$ with $c = 0$.
With no premium the flat part sits on the axis.
$K + c = 100 + 0 = 100$. Above it you gain; you never lose.

feedback.correct: $K + 0 = K$: a free option breaks even at its strike.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $c = 0$ into the break-even.

explain.text: With no premium, profit equals payoff. It is 0 up to the strike and positive above it. So the break-even is the strike itself, and the most you can lose is nothing.

screens.prose: Now a put. You pay $p = \text{£}4.00$ for a put struck at £100.00. Its profit is its payoff less £4.00.
screens.question: Where is the put's break-even?

options.why: You added the premium, as for a call. A put gains as the share falls, so it must end £4.00 below the strike.
You put the break-even at the strike. There the put pays nothing, and you are £4.00 down.
You took the premium off twice. At £92.00 the put pays £8.00, a profit of £4.00.

hints.text: Which way must the share move for a put to pay?
Find where the falling part of the line crosses zero.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A put earns its premium back only as the share falls below the strike.

byKey.plus: You added the premium. That works for calls, which gain as the share rises.

explain.text: A put pays $100 - S_T$ below the strike. That repays the £4.00 premium at $S_T = 96$. So a put's break-even is $K - p$: the premium is subtracted, not added.

screens.prose: Profit is payoff less premium. Break-even is where it is zero: $$\text{call: } K + c, \qquad \text{put: } K - p.$$ We ignore that the premium is paid today but the payoff comes later; over months the interest is small. The diagram says what each price would earn, not how likely it is.
screens.question: A put struck at £80.00 costs £2.50. Where is its break-even?

options.why: You added the premium, the rule for a call. A put's payoff grows as the price falls.
At the strike the put pays nothing, so you are £2.50 down.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $K - p$ for a put.

explain.text: At £77.50 the put pays $80 - 77.50 = 2.50$, exactly its premium. Below that price you profit; above it you lose, at most £2.50.

screens.prose: We found the call's break-even by sliding. Now we derive it, assuming the premium $c$ is positive.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $\max(S_T - K,\ 0) - c = 0$, since profit is zero at break-even
$\max(S_T - K,\ 0) = c > 0$, adding $c$ to both sides
So $S_T > K$, because the max is positive only above the strike
$S_T - K = c$, since above the strike the max equals $S_T - K$
$S_T = K + c$, adding $K$ to both sides

hints.text: Start from what break-even means for the profit.
Before you can drop the max, you must know which side of the strike you are on.
Set profit to zero, move $c$ across, use $c > 0$ to place $S_T$ above $K$, then solve.

feedback.correct: Zero profit, then the side of the strike, then solve.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. You cannot replace the max by $S_T - K$ until you know $S_T > K$.

byKey.d4: Dropping the max needs $S_T > K$ first. Put the line that shows it earlier.
byKey.d3: That conclusion needs the max to equal $c > 0$. It comes after moving $c$ across.

explain.text: The key step is the third: a positive payoff forces $S_T$ above the strike. Only then does the max become $S_T - K$. The same steps for a put give $K - S_T = p$, so $S_T = K - p$.

screens.prose: A share trades at £100.00. You can buy the share, or a call struck at £100.00 for £3.00. The share ends at £110.00, a 10% gain for its owner.
screens.question: What return does the call earn on the £3.00 paid?

hints.text: Return is profit divided by what you paid.
The profit is shown on the label.
$\tfrac{7}{3} \approx 2.333$, about 233%.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the profit by the £3.00 premium.

byKey.payoff: You divided the payoff, £10.00, by £3.00. Take the premium off first: £7.00 of profit.
byKey.share: That is the share's return. The call's profit is measured against £3.00, not £100.00.
byKey.pounds: You divided the profit by the share's price. The call cost only £3.00.

explain.text: The call turns a 10% move into about 233%, because £3.00 controls the gains of a £100.00 share. That is **leverage**. The same lever works against you, as the next screen shows.

screens.prose: Same choice: the share at £100.00, or the call struck at £100.00 for £3.00. Compare the two returns across outcomes. Round to one decimal place.
screens.question: Fill in the call's return for each price at expiry.

hints.text: For each price: payoff, less £3.00, divided by £3.00.
At £90.00 and £100.00 the call pays nothing.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Return is (payoff − 3) ÷ 3, as a percentage.

byKey.r0c2: At £90.00 the call pays 0, so the whole £3.00 is lost: −100%.
byKey.r1c2: A flat share still loses the call buyer everything: the call pays 0 at its strike.

explain.text: The share's returns run from −10% to 20%; the call's from −100% to about 567%. A small move decides between losing everything and multiplying the stake. Leverage magnifies both ways.

ideas: Profit is payoff less premium: the payoff line shifted down by what you paid.
Break-even is $K + c$ for a call and $K - p$ for a put; a buyer can lose at most the premium.
A small premium controls a whole share's gains, so option returns are leveraged both ways.

formula.name: Call profit and break-even
formula.note: For a put: $\max(K - S_T,\ 0) - p$, with break-even $K - p$.

summary.trap: A put's break-even is $K - p$, below the strike. Adding the premium is the call's rule.

quiz.prose: You bought a call struck at £50.00 for £2.40. At expiry the share is at £51.00.
quiz.question: What is your profit?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Payoff first, then take off the premium.

byKey.payoff: That is the payoff. Take off the £2.40 premium.
byKey.added: You added the premium. It was paid, so it comes off.
byKey.premium: You gave the call a payoff of 0. At £51.00 it pays £1.00.

explain.text: The call is exercised and pays $51 - 50 = 1$. Less the £2.40 premium, that is a loss of £1.40. Exercising was still right: it cut the loss from £2.40.

quiz.question: What is its break-even price at expiry?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A put's break-even is below its strike.

byKey.plus: You added the premium, the call's rule. A put needs the share to fall.
byKey.strike: At the strike the put pays nothing.

explain.text: The put pays $30 - S_T$ below the strike, which equals the £1.20 premium at $S_T = 28.80$.

quiz.prose: You buy a put struck at £70.00 for £5.00.
quiz.question: What is the most you can lose?

options.why: You charged yourself the strike. A put buyer never has to sell; above £70.00 they walk away.
That is the break-even price, not a loss.
You described a short call. A buyer's loss stops at the premium.

feedback.correct: The premium is all a buyer can lose.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What is lost if the put is never exercised?

explain.text: If the share ends at or above £70.00 the put pays 0 and the £5.00 premium is gone. That is the worst case, however high the share rises.

quiz.prose: You bought a call struck at £100.00 for £3.00.
quiz.question: Where must the share end for a profit of £5.00?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The payoff must cover the premium and the £5.00.

byKey.no-prem: You forgot the premium. At £105.00 the profit is only £2.00.
byKey.be: That is the break-even, where profit is 0.
byKey.minus: You took the premium off. The share must climb past it.

explain.text: Profit $= (S_T - 100) - 3$ above the strike. Setting it to 5 gives $S_T = 108$: £3.00 to break even, then £5.00 more.
